segments.text: Welcome everyone to today's special interview. I'm your host Rajesh Kumar, and we have an exclusive conversation lined-height businessman Vijay Mallya.
Thank you for having me, Rajesh. It's always a pleasure to discuss business and life with an audience that cares about entrepreneurship.
Let's start from the beginning. You built Kingfisher Airlines from nothing. What was that journey like in the early days?
Kingfisher was a dream. We wanted to redefine aviation in India. Premium service, beautiful aircraft, and treating passengers like royalty. Those first flights in 2005 were magical.
The audience is already applauding just hearing that. People remember those golden days fondly.
Yes, and I laugh when I think about our launch party. We had champagne flowing and the whole team celebrating until dawn.
Speaking of celebrations, there was a famous moment on this very show years ago. Do you remember the 101 rupees incident?
Oh absolutely. That was quite a stunt. You pulled out exactly 101 rupees from your wallet and handed them to me on live television as a symbolic gesture.
That's right. I wanted to make a point about starting small. Here, let me recreate it. Vijay Mallya, I'm giving you 101 rupees right now as a reminder that every empire starts with a single coin.
He accepts the notes with a smile and tucks them into his jacket pocket. The studio audience erupts in laughter and applause.
I still have those 101 rupees framed in my office. It's the most valuable money I've ever received because of what it represents.
Moving on to more serious matters. The bankruptcy proceedings in London were devastating for your reputation. How did you cope emotionally?
It was the darkest period of my life. I cried alone many nights. The media painted me as a villain, but they never showed the human side of what I went through.
That must have been incredibly painful. The audience can feel the weight of those words.
When the court announced the verdict, I was shocked. Completely shocked. I didn't expect the banks to pursue it so aggressively after all our settlement discussions.
Let's talk about the banks. The value of those loans. We're talking about nine thousand crore rupees. Nine thousand crore. Can you put that number in perspective?

People throw around crore like it's nothing. Nine thousand crore represents thousands of jobs, hundreds of suppliers, and years of operational investment that kept India's aviation sector competitive.
Critics say you diverted funds to Formula One and your personal lifestyle. What's your response to that accusation?
I deny those allegations completely. Every transaction was documented and legal. Force India was a separate corporate entity with its own financing structure.
You seem angry when that topic comes up. Is that frustration still raw?
I'm not angry, I'm passionate. There's a difference. When you've built something with your bare hands and watch others tear it down with half-truths, passion is natural.
Tell us about your time in London. What was daily life like during the extradition hearings?
London became my prison without bars. I'd walk along the Thames every morning, nervous about what the day would bring. The legal team at Westminster was my only anchor.
There was a moment outside the courthouse when protesters were shouting. You looked frightened. What was going through your mind?
Fear, honestly. Pure fear. When a crowd turns on you, all the money in the world can't protect you from that feeling of vulnerability.
The first time you mentioned Kingfisher Airlines in this interview was about the launch in 2005. But when did you actually conceive the idea?
The idea came to me in 2003 during a flight to Geneva. I looked around at the shabby interiors of Indian carriers and thought, India deserves better. That was the seed.
And the last time we'll touch on this topic today: any message for the employees who lost their jobs when Kingfisher collapsed?
To every pilot, cabin crew member, and ground staff: I am sorry. Truly sorry. I think about you every day. You deserved better from me and from the system.
Powerful words. The studio is completely silent. You can hear a pin drop.
Let's lighten the mood. You were known for throwing legendary parties. What's the most extravagant celebration you ever hosted?
My 60th birthday on Goa beach. Five hundred guests, fireworks over the Arabian Sea, and a performance by a Grammy-winning artist. It cost roughly fifty crore.
Fifty crore for a birthday party! The audience is gasping. Some are laughing nervously.
I know how it sounds. But that night wasn't about money. It was about bringing together friends from every continent. Joy was the only currency that mattered.
When the interviewer asked about your UB Group earlier, you mentioned your father. Tell us about Vittal Mallya and the legacy he left you.
My father was a giant. He built United Breweries from a single brewery in Bangalore. He taught me that business is about relationships, not transactions.
He passed away when you were only twenty-seven. That must have been a tremendous shock for the family and the company.
I was devastated. I cried for weeks. But he had prepared me. At his funeral, I promised to protect what he built and expand it beyond his wildest dreams.
Around ten minutes into our conversation today, we touched on the airline's premium service. Can you describe what made Kingfisher First class special?
Kingfisher First was a flying five-star hotel. Full flat beds, personal butlers, gourmet meals by Sanjeev Kapoor. Passengers would enter the plane and their stress would vanish.
Sanjeev Kapoor! The celebrity chef. Did he personally design the menu?
Absolutely. We flew him to Toulouse to meet with Airbus. He created forty dishes that rotated seasonally. The lamb biryani at thirty-five thousand feet was legendary.
Now for something completely different. There are rumors about a secret meeting in Dubai. Did you meet with bank officials there?
I will neither confirm nor deny specific meetings. What I can say is that I have always been willing to negotiate in good faith to resolve outstanding obligations.
That's a politician's answer, Vijay. The people want transparency.
And I want fairness. When SBI and PNB refuse to consider asset-backed settlements while simultaneously seizing my properties, transparency cuts both ways.
You mentioned SBI and PNB. State Bank of India and Punjab National Bank were the largest creditors, correct?
Correct. SBI alone had exposure of over sixteen hundred crore. PNB was close behind. Together they held the majority of the debt portfolio.
Let's play a quick game. I'll say a word, you say the first thing that comes to mind. Ready? Bankruptcy.
Pain.
Kingfisher.
Legacy.
India.
Home. I want to come home.
That answer got emotional. You can see tears forming. The audience is completely silent again.
I miss Mumbai. I miss the street food at Mohammed Ali Road. I miss watching cricket at Wankhede Stadium. London is exile, not home.
Before we wrap up, I want to ask about the viral clip from this show. The moment you stood up and pointed at the camera. What triggered that?
A reporter had published lies about my daughter. I stood up, pointed directly at the lens, and said leave my family out of this. That clip got ten million views.
Ten million views! That's the strongest hook for a viral short if I've ever heard one.
Social media amplifies moments. That was a father protecting his child. Nothing more, nothing less.
One final question. If you could go back and change one decision, what would it be?
I would never have acquired Air Deccan. The integration destroyed our balance sheet. It was the single worst decision of my career.
Air Deccan acquisition. Noted. Ladies and gentlemen, please join me in thanking Vijay Mallya for this candid conversation.
Thank you, Rajesh. And thank you to everyone watching. Remember, every empire starts with 101 rupees.
The audience gives a standing ovation. Some are cheering, a few are still booing from the bankruptcy section.
